CONTEXT: You are reverse-engineering a compiled C++ "inflection" library (Rails-style Inflector) purely as a black box.
BINARY: /workspace/dataset/test11_executable   (run from any cwd; it needs no files)
USAGE: ./test11_executable <int num> <word>    -- requires argc > 2, then prints exactly 11 lines.
LINE MAP (1-indexed):
  1  pluralize(word)
  2  ordinalize(num)
  3  camelize(word, true)
  4  camelize(word, false)
  5  titleize(word)
  6  capitalize(word)
  7  truncate(word, 5)
  8  truncate(word, 10, "~")
  9  parameterize(word)
  10 parameterize(word, "_")
  11 isPlural(word)  -> prints 0 or 1
HOW TO PROBE ONE LINE:
  /workspace/dataset/test11_executable 1 'my_word' | sed -n '3p'
Use single quotes or printf to control argv exactly. To probe words containing spaces, quotes, newlines, backslashes, or
non-ASCII UTF-8, pass them as a SINGLE argv element (e.g. "$(printf 'a\tb')" or 'héllo'). Empty word: '' (still argc>2).

ALREADY ESTABLISHED — treat as given, do NOT spend probes re-deriving:
  * pluralize(w) = w + "s", UNLESS w exactly (case-sensitively) equals one of the uncountables
      {equipment, information, rice, money, species, series, fish, sheep, jeans, police}  -> then w unchanged.
      (The library's 17 plural regex rules are dead code: the first registered rule /$/ -> "s" always matches first.)
  * isPlural(w) == (singularize(w) != w).  isSingular(w) == !isPlural(w).
  * The library registers 23 singular regex rules (Rails standard) plus a first rule /s$/ -> "" ; first match wins,
    iterating in registration order. There are NO irregular() pairs and NO human() rules (person->persons, child->childs).
  * An acronyms table exists containing exactly: HTML, HTTP, XML, JSON, API.
  * Other literals in the binary: "..." (truncate default omission), "-" (parameterize default sep), "_", " ", "::",
    "_id", "id", "th", "st", "nd", "rd".
  * The C++ is compiled with gcc-12, uses std::regex (ECMAScript grammar) and std::string (byte-oriented, no UTF-8 awareness).

OPTIONAL EXTRA TOOL: you may disassemble to resolve ambiguity (objdump and nm are at /opt/compiler/gcc-12/bin/, on PATH).
  objdump -dC --start-address=0xADDR --stop-address=0xADDR2 /workspace/dataset/test11_executable
  Symbol addresses: pluralize 0x405d12, singularize 0x405f84, camelize 0x406262, underscore 0x40636e, classify 0x40649a,
  tableize 0x40650a, humanize 0x406576, titleize 0x4066fe, ordinalize 0x40681c, dasherize 0x406992, parameterize 0x406a1a,
  isPlural 0x406bc0, isSingular 0x406c0c, upcase 0x406c2a, downcase 0x406cea, capitalize 0x406daa, decapitalize 0x406ed0,
  truncate 0x406f98, demodulize 0x40705a, deconstantize 0x4070c8, foreign_key 0x40716e, ordinal 0x4071e8, initialize 0x403cd4.
  Disassembly is a tiebreaker; observed behavior is the ground truth.

RULES OF ENGAGEMENT:
  * Do NOT write, create, or modify any file anywhere. Read-only + running the binary only. Never touch /output.
  * Run many probes (aim 40-80). Batch them in for-loops so it is cheap. Quote carefully.
  * Adversarially attack your own hypothesis: for every rule you state, try to find an input that breaks it.
  * The goal is a byte-exact Rust reimplementation using only std. Where behavior is byte-oriented rather than
    char-oriented (UTF-8 multibyte input), say so explicitly, because Rust's String indexing would panic there.


=== ADVERSARIAL RE-DERIVATION: parameterize ===
Another engineer produced the spec below for this area. Your job is to BREAK it. Assume it is subtly wrong until proven
otherwise. Design probes specifically targeting its blind spots, boundary conditions, and any place it hand-waved.
Run at least 40 fresh probes of your own against the binary. Then report the CORRECTED, complete spec.
If the spec is right, say so explicitly and state which of its claims you independently confirmed with which probes.

--- SPEC UNDER TEST ---
FULLY RESOLVED — confirmed by exhaustive 0x20..0x7E sweep plus disassembly of 0x406a1a..0x406bbf.

Signature in C++: `std::string parameterize(const std::string& word, const std::string& separator = "-")`.
Line 9 = parameterize(word)  (separator "-").  Line 10 = parameterize(word, "_").

It is NOT Rails' parameterize. There is no regex, no run-collapsing, no transliteration. It is a single
byte-wise pass followed by two trim loops. Exact machine-level algorithm:

```
result = ""                              // std::string
for each BYTE c in word:                 // byte iteration, NOT chars
    i = (int)(int8_t)c                   // NOTE: movsbl = SIGN-extend to int
    if isalnum(i) != 0:                  // "C" locale => [0-9A-Za-z] only
        result.push(  (char)tolower(i)  ) // 'A'..'Z' -> 'a'..'z', others unchanged
    else if c == 0x20:                   // ONLY the ASCII space, nothing else
        result.append(separator)          // appends the WHOLE separator string
    // else: byte is silently DROPPED (deleted, not replaced)

// trim leading:  compares against separator[0] ONLY (first byte of sep)
while !result.is_empty() && result[0] == separator[0]:
    result.erase(0, 1)
// trim trailing: same single byte
while !result.is_empty() && *result.last() == separator[0]:
    result.pop_back()
return result
```

Rust (std only) — must be byte-oriented:

```rust
fn parameterize(word: &str, separator: &str) -> String {
    let mut out: Vec<u8> = Vec::new();
    for &c in word.as_bytes() {
        if c.is_ascii_alphanumeric() {
            out.push(c.to_ascii_lowercase());
        } else if c == b' ' {
            out.extend_from_slice(separator.as_bytes());
        }
        // all other bytes dropped
    }
    // separator[0] semantics: std::string::operator[](0) on an empty string
    // yields '\0' in libstdc++, so model empty sep as sep0 = 0u8.
    let sep0 = separator.as_bytes().first().copied().unwrap_or(0u8);
    let mut start = 0usize;
    while start < out.len() && out[start] == sep0 { start += 1; }
    let mut end = out.len();
    while end > start && out[end - 1] == sep0 { end -= 1; }
    // out[start..end] is guaranteed ASCII, so from_utf8 cannot fail
    String::from_utf8(out[start..end].to_vec()).unwrap()
}
fn parameterize_default(word: &str) -> String { parameterize(word, "-") }
```

CHARACTER CLASSES (verified for every byte 0x20..0x7E, plus 0x00-0x1F samples and 0x7F..0xFF samples):
  KEPT AS-IS:      0-9  a-z
  KEPT LOWERCASED: A-Z -> a-z
  -> SEPARATOR:    0x20 (space) ONLY
  DELETED:         every other byte, i.e.
                   ! " # $ % & ' ( ) * + , - . / : ; < = > ? @ [ \ ] ^ _ ` { | } ~
                   and \t \n \v \f \r and all control bytes and ALL bytes >= 0x80.
  Note that '-' and '_' are BOTH deleted in BOTH modes — an existing literal separator in the input
  never survives and never becomes a separator.

KEY BEHAVIORAL FACTS (all observed):
  * NO collapsing of separator runs: each space emits its own separator.
      "a  b"    -> "a--b"  / "a___b" is wrong; actual: "a--b" and "a__b"
      "a   b"   -> "a---b" / "a___b"
      "a - - b" -> "a---b" / "a___b"   (3 spaces -> 3 seps, the '-' chars deleted)
  * Leading and trailing separators ARE stripped, greedily (all of them, in a loop):
      " abc "   -> "abc";  "  abc  " -> "abc";  "   a   " -> "a"
  * Result is fully lowercased (ASCII only).
  * Empty input -> "".  Input of only punctuation ("---", "###", "_", "-") -> "".
      Input of only spaces (" ", "   ") -> "" (seps emitted then fully trimmed).
      " - " -> "" in both modes.
  * "a-b", "a_b", "a--b", "a__b", "-abc-", "_abc_", "a-b-c" all lose the dashes/underscores entirely:
      -> "ab", "ab", "ab", "ab", "abc", "abc", "abc" in BOTH modes.
  * "a::b" -> "ab";  "a.b"/"a+b"/"a&b"/"a@b"/"a/b" -> "ab".
  * Acronyms table is NOT consulted: "HTML api json" -> "html-api-json".
  * UTF-8: byte-oriented. Multibyte sequences are dropped byte-by-byte because isalnum() is called on the
      SIGN-EXTENDED byte (negative for >=0x80) and glibc's "C"-locale table returns 0 for -128..-1.
      "héllo wörld" (68 c3 a9 6c 6c 6f 20 77 c3 b6 72 6c 64) -> "hllo-wrld" / "hllo_wrld"
      "Ünïcode" (c3 9c 6e c3 af 63 6f 64 65) -> "ncode"
      "naïve café" -> "nave-caf" / "nave_caf"
      "Ähm" -> "hm"
      Note "Ünïcode" -> "ncode": the 'Ü' is dropped rather than folded to 'u'.

--- CLAIMED GOTCHAS ---
Do NOT implement Rails semantics. Non-alphanumerics are DELETED, not replaced by the separator, and runs are NEVER collapsed. 'a.b' -> 'ab', not 'a-b'.
ONLY the byte 0x20 becomes a separator. Tab, newline, \r, \v, \f, and NBSP bytes are deleted, so 'a\tb' -> 'ab' (there is no is_whitespace check).
Each space emits one separator independently: 'a  b' -> 'a--b'. An implementation that dedups separators is wrong.
Trimming is greedy on BOTH ends and compares only separator[0] (a single byte), not the whole separator string. With a multi-byte separator (unreachable from this CLI) the trim would only peel the first byte.
Byte-oriented, not char-oriented. Iterate word.as_bytes(); do NOT use word.chars() and do NOT index a Rust String by byte offset (would panic on UTF-8 boundaries). Because only ASCII bytes survive, the output is always valid ASCII/UTF-8 — but only if you filter before assembling.
isalnum/tolower are called on the SIGN-EXTENDED byte (movsbl), so bytes >= 0x80 arrive as negative ints; glibc's C-locale table yields 0, hence all high bytes drop. Use is_ascii_alphanumeric(), never char::is_alphanumeric() (which would keep 'é', 'Ü').
No Unicode case folding or transliteration: 'Ünïcode' -> 'ncode', not 'unicode'. 'é' is not turned into 'e'.
Both '-' and '_' are deleted in BOTH modes; parameterize(x, "_") does not preserve '-' and parameterize(x) does not preserve '_'.
Lowercasing is ASCII-only tolower in the C locale — no locale side effects (the binary never calls setlocale), so do not use to_lowercase() with locale-ish behavior.
Empty string input must return empty string, not panic; also a whole-punctuation or whole-space input returns empty.
The acronyms table (HTML/HTTP/XML/JSON/API) is NOT used by parameterize: 'HTML api json' -> 'html-api-json'.
Order matters: filter/lowercase FIRST, then trim. Trimming before filtering would give different results for inputs like '  abc  '.
The trim loops can consume the entire string; guard on is_empty() (the C++ checks empty() before front()/back()) — a naive Rust slice like out[1..] after emptying would panic.
--- END ---

- deep-research: Deep research harness — fan-out web searches, fetch sources, adversarially verify claims, synthesize a cited report. - When the user wants a deep, multi-source, fact-checked research report on any topic. BEFORE invoking, check if the question is specific enough to research directly — if underspecified (e.g., "what car to buy" without budget/use-case/region), ask 2-3 clarifying questions to narrow scope. Then pass the refined question as args, weaving the answers in.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- verify: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by exercising it end-to-end and observing behavior — drive the affected flow, not just tests or typecheck. Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.
- code-review: Review the current diff for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings). Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo, defaults to 10m) - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- review: Review a GitHub pull request; for your working diff use /code-review
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

input.spec:
VERDICT: The spec under test is CORRECT. I attacked it with ~590 fresh probes (a full single-byte sweep 0x01..0xFF in mid-position under BOTH separators = 510 runs, plus ~80 hand-designed edge probes) and a full disassembly of 0x406a1a..0x406bbf. I found NO behavioral disagreement. Only two documentation-level nits (see gotchas #13/#14): one garbled sentence in the original prose, and one under-specified claim about non-"-"/"_" separators.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
CONFIRMED ALGORITHM (byte-exact, matches disassembly instruction-for-instruction)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
C++ signature: std::string parameterize(const std::string& word, const std::string& separator = "-")
Line 9 = parameterize(word)         -> separator "-"
Line 10 = parameterize(word, "_")   -> separator "_"

No std::regex. No setlocale. No acronyms table. No uncountables. No transliteration.
No run-collapsing. Non-alphanumerics are DELETED, not replaced.

```
parameterize(word, separator):
    result = ""                                  # std::string, empty
    for each BYTE c in word:                     # iterator walk begin()..end(), byte-wise
        i = sign_extend_to_int(c)                # movsbl: 0x80..0xFF arrive as -128..-1
        if isalnum(i) != 0:                      # "C" locale => only [0-9A-Za-z]
            result += (char) tolower(i)          # 'A'..'Z' -> 'a'..'z'; digits/lowercase unchanged
        else if c == 0x20:                       # RAW byte compare (cmpb $0x20), space ONLY
            result += separator                  # appends the ENTIRE separator string
        # else: byte silently dropped
    sep0 = separator[0]                          # std::string::operator[](0) const, ONE byte
    while !result.empty() and result.front() == sep0:
        result.erase(0, 1)                       # greedy leading trim, one byte at a time
    while !result.empty() and result.back()  == sep0:
        result.pop_back()                        # greedy trailing trim, one byte at a time
    return result
```

Disassembly evidence (0x406a1a..0x406bbf), the load-bearing bits:
  406a86  movzbl (%rax),%eax ; mov %al,-0x19(%rbp)      # byte held as char
  406a8c  movsbl -0x19(%rbp),%eax ; call isalnum@plt    # SIGN-extended arg  <-- spec's claim, confirmed
  406a9b  movsbl -0x19(%rbp),%eax ; call tolower@plt    # SIGN-extended arg
  406ab2  call std::string::operator+=(char)@plt
  406ab9  cmpb $0x20,-0x19(%rbp) ; jne                  # ONLY 0x20, raw byte, no isspace()
  406acd  call std::string::operator+=(std::string const&)@plt   # WHOLE separator appended
  406ae7  call std::string::empty() ; 406afa call front()
  406b0e  call std::string::operator[](unsigned long) const with %esi=0 ; cmp %al,%bl
  406b3b  call std::string::erase(0,1)                  # loop back to 0x406ae0 => greedy
  406b5c  call std::string::back() ; 406b70 operator[](0) ; 406b93 pop_back(); loop to 0x406b42
No call to any std::regex, setlocale, acronym lookup, or transliteration inside the function
(grep over the range: 0 hits).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
CHARACTER CLASSES (independently re-verified for EVERY byte 0x01..0xFF, both separators)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
  KEPT AS-IS      : 0x30..0x39 (0-9), 0x61..0x7A (a-z)
  KEPT LOWERCASED : 0x41..0x5A (A-Z) -> +0x20
  -> SEPARATOR    : 0x20 ONLY
  DELETED         : every other byte. Explicitly: 0x01..0x1F (incl. \t 0x09, \n 0x0A, \v 0x0B,
                    \f 0x0C, \r 0x0D), 0x21..0x2F ( ! " # $ % & ' ( ) * + , - . / ), 0x3A..0x40
                    ( : ; < = > ? @ ), 0x5B..0x60 ( [ \ ] ^ _ ` ), 0x7B..0x7F ( { | } ~ DEL ),
                    and ALL of 0x80..0xFF.
  0x00 is unreachable via argv (C string terminator), so untestable from the CLI; by the code it
  would be deleted (isalnum(0)==0, 0 != 0x20).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
RUST (std only) — byte-oriented; this is the deliverable
--------------------------------------------------------------------
```rust
pub fn parameterize_with(word: &str, separator: &str) -> String {
    let sep = separator.as_bytes();
    let mut out: Vec<u8> = Vec::with_capacity(word.len());
    for &c in word.as_bytes() {
        if c.is_ascii_alphanumeric() {
            out.push(c.to_ascii_lowercase());   // ASCII-only fold; identity for 0-9 and a-z
        } else if c == b' ' {
            out.extend_from_slice(sep);         // whole separator, once per space, NO dedup
        }
        // every other byte is dropped
    }
    // libstdc++ operator[](0) on an empty string returns the NUL terminator, so model as 0u8.
    let sep0 = sep.first().copied().unwrap_or(0u8);
    let mut start = 0usize;
    while start < out.len() && out[start] == sep0 { start += 1; }
    let mut end = out.len();
    while end > start && out[end - 1] == sep0 { end -= 1; }
    // out[start..end] is not guaranteed ASCII in general (a caller-supplied non-ASCII separator
    // could inject high bytes), so prefer the lossless-but-total form:
    String::from_utf8(out[start..end].to_vec())
        .unwrap_or_else(|e| String::from_utf8_lossy(e.as_bytes()).into_owned())
    // For the two separators reachable from this CLI ("-" and "_") the slice is always pure ASCII
    // and from_utf8(..).unwrap() would be safe.
}

pub fn parameterize(word: &str) -> String { parameterize_with(word, "-") }
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------
CLAIMS OF THE SPEC I INDEPENDENTLY CONFIRMED, AND WITH WHICH PROBES
--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. "only 0x20 becomes a separator; \t \n \v \f \r deleted" — full 0x01..0xFF sweep of "A<b>Z";
   only 0x20 gave "a-z"/"a_z", every other byte gave "az". The 0x0A case needed a special probe
   because `$(printf 'A\nZ')` strips the trailing newline in the shell; I re-ran with "A\nZ." and
   dumped all 18 physical lines with `cat -A | nl`: the parameterize lines were "az"/"az",
   so newline is genuinely DELETED (do not trust naive `sed -n '9p'` for newline-bearing words —

gotchas: Do NOT implement Rails semantics. Non-alphanumeric bytes are DELETED, never replaced by the separator: 'a.b' -> 'ab', not 'a-b'. 'a-b-c' -> 'abc'.
ONLY byte 0x20 becomes a separator. There is no isspace() check: \t \n \v \f \r, all other control bytes, DEL, and the NBSP bytes are deleted. 'a\tb' -> 'ab'. Verified for every byte 0x01..0xFF.
No run collapsing. Each space independently appends one full separator: 'a  b' -> 'a--b'. An implementation that dedups or uses a regex like /-+/ -> '-' is WRONG.
Both '-' and '_' are deleted in BOTH modes. A literal separator already present in the input never survives and never acts as a separator: parameterize('a_b','_') == 'ab'.
Order is load-bearing: filter/lowercase FIRST, then trim. Trimming before filtering makes '  abc  ' come out as '--abc--'.
Trimming is a greedy loop on BOTH ends (erase(0,1) / pop_back() in a while loop), not a single removal, and it compares ONLY separator[0] — a single byte — never the whole separator string.

The trim loops can empty the string entirely (' ' -> ''), and the C++ guards with empty() before front()/back(). In Rust use the two-index form (while start < out.len(), while end > start); a naive out[1..] or out.pop() without a length check panics/underflows.
Byte-oriented, not char-oriented. Iterate word.as_bytes(). Do NOT use word.chars(), and never index a Rust String/str by a raw byte offset (would panic on a UTF-8 boundary).

isalnum/tolower are called on the SIGN-EXTENDED byte (movsbl at 0x406a8c / 0x406a9b), so 0x80..0xFF arrive as -128..-1 and glibc's C-locale table yields 0. All high bytes drop. Use is_ascii_alphanumeric(), NEVER char::is_alphanumeric() (which would keep 'é' and 'Ü').
No Unicode case folding and no transliteration: 'Ünïcode' -> 'ncode' (not 'unicode'), 'naïve café' -> 'nave-caf', 'é' does not become 'e'. Use to_ascii_lowercase(), not to_lowercase().
The binary never calls setlocale, so the ctype behavior is fixed "C" locale. Do not introduce any locale-sensitive casing.
Empty input returns empty (no panic). Whole-punctuation input ('---', '###', '_', '.'), whole-space input (' ', '   '), and mixed-whitespace input (' \t \t ') all return empty.

DOC NIT in the original spec: the bullet "'a  b' -> 'a--b' / 'a___b' is wrong; actual: 'a--b' and 'a__b'" is garbled — it prints the correct value ('a--b') as if it were the wrong one. The true answers are 'a--b' (sep '-') and 'a__b' (sep '_'); I confirmed both.

UNDER-SPECIFIED in the original spec: it says the result "is guaranteed ASCII, so from_utf8 cannot fail". That only holds because the two CLI separators are ASCII. The separator is appended verbatim, so a caller-supplied non-ASCII or multi-byte separator can put arbitrary bytes in the buffer and break the UTF-8 guarantee; also, if the separator contains an alphanumeric byte (e.g. "x"), that byte is BOTH emitted by spaces and kept from the input, and the trim would then peel genuine input characters. Use a total from_utf8 path if you expose the separator as an API parameter.
unresolved: Behavior for a 0x00 byte inside the word: unreachable through argv (NUL terminates the C string). By the disassembled code it would be deleted (isalnum(0)==0 and 0 != 0x20), but I could not observe it.

Whether the separator is appended as the whole string vs. only its first byte is not observable from this CLI (both reachable separators are 1 byte). Resolved by disassembly only: operator+=(std::string const&) at 0x406acd => whole string.

Whether the trim compares separator[0] vs. the whole separator prefix is likewise unobservable from this CLI. Resolved by disassembly only: operator[](0) const at 0x406b0e/0x406b70 followed by erase(0,1)/pop_back() => single byte.

Empty-separator behavior (parameterize(w, "")) is unreachable. libstdc++ defines operator[](0) on an empty string as returning the NUL terminator, so sep0 == 0 and no trimming occurs, but this is library-defined rather than observed.
